title: DevRel, Part 5: Bad news and crises - speak before you are asked
subtitle: The sequence for handling an incident, how to write a bad-news announcement, and why drip-feeding is the worst approach
whyItMatters: Every DevRel team does well when things go smoothly. The job proves its worth in the week of an incident, and what gets done that week decides whether the product loses a week or loses years of trust.
openingQuestion: You find that an authorisation bug exposed some accounts' data through the API for three weeks. How should it be disclosed?
openingOptions: Establish the scope, then disclose it all at once
Announce what is known now and update as the review continues
Patch it quietly in the next release with a one-line technical note
Wait for an independent security firm to confirm, then publish with its report
explanation: You need a short window to learn how far the bug reached - how many accounts, which kinds of data, since when - and then disclose it whole, once. This is one of the rare exceptions to disclosing as early as possible, and the reason is how users react to drip-fed news: with each update adding another piece, they do not add the new piece on, they reopen the question of how much is still unknown - so three small announcements do far more damage than one complete announcement with the same content. But that window must be measured in hours or a few days, not weeks - for personal data it is also capped by the legal 72-hour deadline - and before anything else, the hole must be closed.

diagram.label: Close the hole and revoke exposed keys immediately
Establish scope - in hours, not weeks
Disclose it whole, once: what, how much, why, how it is being fixed
Follow up and answer, without changing the story

realWorldExample.company: Post-incident reviews published in the open
realWorldExample.description: When a cloud provider publishes a post-incident review whose scope is much larger than its first notice, users react far more strongly than the gap in the numbers would justify. The reason is that they read that gap as a signal about the provider's own monitoring - and once they doubt that, every other number on the status page gets doubted too.

quiz.question: Why does drip-feeding disclosure do more damage than a single disclosure?
options: Because email costs rise with each send
Because the rules forbid disclosing one matter in several announcements
Because the press will cover it repeatedly and amplify how serious it is
Because every update makes users ask how much is still unknown
quiz.explanation: Users do not add up the pieces of bad news; they re-assess the uncertainty. Drip-feeding keeps that uncertainty from ever closing, so each new piece lands as a fresh shock rather than a small addition to a known total.

quiz.question: What is the first thing to do on discovering a material security incident?
options: Close the hole and revoke the exposed keys
Draft a press release to take control of the message
Tell the large customers first
Review the entire related security testing process
quiz.explanation: From the moment someone knows, the hole is still open and may still be being exploited. Every minute it stays open while an announcement is drafted turns one incident into two - and closing it takes minutes and does not require knowing the scope.

quiz.question: What should a bad-news announcement contain that a poor one usually lacks?
options: An apology addressed to users
Concrete figures and the known dates, even when incomplete
A commitment that it will never happen again in future
A comparison showing similar products have the same problem
quiz.explanation: Poor announcements are full of adjectives and commitments. Users need to know how many accounts were affected, over what period, and who is handling it - the rest is words.

quiz.question: Why should you not promise 'it will never happen again'?
options: Because users will demand compensation from the company if it recurs
Because the rules do not allow a business to make commitments about the future
Because it is a promise nobody controls, and a recurrence will cost twice as much
Because that promise forces the testing firm to widen its review
quiz.explanation: Being able to say specifically which control was changed is far better than an absolute promise - that promise only creates one more place to break your word.

quiz.question: After disclosure, what matters most in the following weeks?
options: Meeting each large customer privately to explain the background in detail
Pushing news of new features
Saying as little as possible so the matter stops being mentioned online
Keeping the story unchanged and updating on exactly the dates promised
quiz.explanation: Changing the story midway does more damage than the original bad news, because it says the first version was incomplete.

practicePrompt.question: A material security incident is discovered at 8am, and the extent of the damage has not yet been established. What is the first thing to do?
options: Close the hole and revoke exposed keys, before drafting any notice
Draft a notice at once and post it on the status page within the hour
Wait until the scope is established before telling engineering leadership
Contact a few friendly customers first to gauge how they will react
practicePrompt.explanation: From the moment anyone in the company knows, every minute the hole stays open is another minute in which data may keep being taken - and closing the hole and revoking exposed keys can be done in minutes, without knowing the extent of the damage. Drafting a notice takes time and establishing scope takes longer, but neither may happen while the door is still open. Only then comes the second principle: establish the scope and disclose it WHOLE, once, because drip-feeding means the uncertainty never closes and every update becomes a new shock.

keyTakeaways: Close the hole and revoke exposed keys as soon as you know - before drafting any notice.
Establish scope and disclose it whole, once; drip-feeding means the uncertainty never closes.
A good announcement has figures and dates, not adjectives and absolute promises.
After disclosure, keep the story unchanged and update on the dates you promised.

summary.keyIdea: Establish the scope and disclose it whole in one go - drip-feeding means the uncertainty never closes
summary.commonMistake: Disclosing the certain part first to reassure people, then revealing another piece each week. Every extra piece resets trust from the beginning.
summary.action: When an incident occurs, the first task is to close the hole and revoke exposed keys - before drafting anything at all.

application.title: Draft an incident notice as practice
application.message: Pick a hypothetical incident and write the notice for it: what happened, the scope in figures, what is being done, and when the next update comes. Then delete every adjective and read it again.
application.secondary: A notice that still stands up once the adjectives are gone is a notice with substance.

sections.text: Every DevRel team looks good in a smooth quarter. The job is proved in the week of an incident - and most of the damage in that week comes from how it was handled, not from the incident itself.

items: Close the hole and revoke exposed keys and sessions immediately. This comes first, before you even know how large the matter is.
Establish the scope: how many accounts, which data, since when, what has not yet been reviewed.
Disclose it whole, once, with dates attached to whatever is still outstanding.
After that, update only on the dates you promised - nothing added, nothing changed.

sections.text: Why drip-feeding is the worst approach

Users do not add up the pieces of bad news. Each time another piece arrives, they reopen the question of how much is still unknown - and that question has no floor. Three small announcements with the same content do far more damage than one complete announcement, because after a complete announcement the uncertainty closes.

left.label: A poor announcement
left.text: Full of adjectives, apologies and promises it will not recur. No figures, no dates, no word on who is handling it.

right.label: A good announcement
right.text: How many accounts were affected, over what period, what the cause was, which control has changed, and when the next information will come.

sections.label: The promise not to make
sections.text: "This will never happen again" is a promise nobody controls, and if it does happen again the second time costs twice as much, because the promise is standing there. Replace it with what you can say specifically: which control has just been added, who approves which step from now on.

lines: An incident costs trust once. Mishandling an incident costs trust again and again.
And what is lost the second time is not bought back with one smooth quarter.
